questions.learningObjective: Identify the rural reference temperature used to define an urban heat island
questions.stem: In an amateur astronomer's log for 12 March, the city centre reads 4.2 C warmer than the rural station at 02:00.

options.text: The rural station temperature is the reference against which the urban heat island is measured
The city centre temperature is the reference for the rural heat island effect
options.misconception: reverses urban and rural reference roles

options.text: The average of both stations is the reference for the heat island
The warmest station of the night is the reference for the heat island
options.misconception: uses an extreme value as baseline

questions.explanation: An urban heat island is measured against a rural reference site, not the city itself or an average. The tempting idea that the city is the baseline reverses the comparison.
questions.hint: Compare the city to the countryside, not to itself.

questions.topic: Heat wave and the nights that do not cool
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a heat wave's danger rises when nights fail to cool
questions.stem: An amateur astronomer's log for 19 July records city minimum temperatures of 28, 29 and 30 C across three nights of a heat wave.

options.text: Warm nights reduce solar radiation so daytime heat feels worse
options.misconception: confuses night warmth with daytime solar load

options.text: Each night failing to cool below 27 C stops the body from recovering heat stress
Minimum temperatures matter only for plants not for human health
Rising minima show the heat wave is already ending

questions.explanation: When nights do not cool, the body cannot shed accumulated heat, compounding daytime stress. Warm nights are not about solar radiation or a sign the wave is ending.
questions.hint: Recovery from heat happens at night.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish deaths explained by heat from those merely coincident
questions.stem: An amateur astronomer's log for August notes 40 extra deaths during a heat wave and asks how many are truly caused by heat.

answer.exemplar: A heat wave causes deaths through direct heat stress and by worsening chronic illness, but not every extra death in that week is attributable to heat; some would have occurred anyway. The excess-mortality method compares observed deaths with the seasonal baseline to estimate the true attributable number.

questions.explanation: Heat waves raise mortality through direct stress and by aggravating chronic disease, yet baseline deaths still occur. Excess mortality above the seasonal baseline estimates the attributable share.
questions.hint: Compare observed deaths with the usual seasonal baseline.

questions.stem: An amateur astronomer's log for 22 November asks why a storm surge on top of a high tide is worse than on a low tide.

questions.topic: Consecutive night minima during a heat wave
questions.learningObjective: Explain why consecutive warm nights compound risk
questions.stem: An amateur astronomer's log for 9 July asks why three warm nights in a row are worse than three scattered warm nights.

answer.exemplar: Consecutive warm nights deny the body any recovery window, so heat stress accumulates day after day. Scattered warm nights allow cooler nights between, giving the body time to reset.

questions.explanation: Back-to-back warm nights remove recovery time and let heat stress build. Scattered nights allow reset. The wrong idea is that only the count matters.
questions.hint: Recovery windows between warm nights matter.

answer.exemplar: Consecutive warm nights signal that the body cannot recover between hot days, so stress accumulates and health risk rises. A single warm night allows recovery and is less dangerous.
